prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength realise optical clocks of unprecedented stability and accuracy

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part, B040, for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Having read all eight statements and the chair's questions, my reasons now rest less on how many members ranked it and more on the one-sentence answer to the chair's first question. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb, a tool for counting optical cycles; the 2012 prize honoured control of individual quantum systems, which is the route to single-ion clocks. The lattice clock adds a third and different thing: the magic-wavelength condition, which cancels the trap-induced shift of the clock transition and therefore lets a large ensemble of neutral atoms be interrogated at once. That is what combined ion-class accuracy with the statistical power of many atoms, and it is what brought independent laboratories to agreement near 1e-18. I read this as a theory-shaped idea, an exact cancellation of a perturbation, followed by an experimental realisation that made it decisive. For the citation I favour the species-neutral wording around the magic-wavelength lattice and the optical lattice clock itself, rather than naming strontium, so that it does not turn into a priority dispute over which atom was first. The redefinition of the second should stay out of the citation because it has not happened; the demonstrated invention and its reproduced performance carry the case on their own.
statement.case_against: Distinctness from 2005 and 2012 is still the main objection, and I cannot rule out that some readers will see a third precision-spectroscopy prize in one lineage. A two-name credit also sets aside Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, and the supplied evidence does not settle how the concept should be divided between Katori and Ye. Katori's role is the concept and first strontium realisation, Ye's the accuracy and stability frontier, but I am a condensed-matter theorist and must lean on the atomic physicists here to judge priority. Last, part of the long-term impact, a redefined second and chronometric geodesy, is still prospective, so the citation must not borrow from it.

responses.point: Danielsson alone prefers B018, IceCube, for Halzen and Karle: a discovery of a diffuse high-energy neutrino flux that nature supplied unexpectedly, opening a new observational channel. He lists B040 as his first alternative and names unresolved source identification and the missing AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers as his own reservations.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-invention distinction seriously. I see why a signal nobody predicted, in a new channel, appeals as a discovery in the strict sense. But the two reservations you list are exactly the ones that weigh on me. The prize would honour a diffuse flux whose sources are still not identified, with KM3NeT and Baikal confirmation still arriving, and a two-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds omits the AMANDA lineage you mention, which you say you have not been able to verify. The lattice clock has the opposite profile: the claim is narrow, already reproduced across many laboratories, and the credit is compact. I would not call B040 a refinement either, since the magic-wavelength condition is a new principle. Because you rate B040 first among your alternatives and would not object strongly, I do not ask you to abandon your reading of B018. I do think its maturity and attribution are less settled than those of B040 this year, so I keep B018 only as an alternative.

responses.point: Kroll supports B040 with Katori credited for the concept and first strontium lattice clocks and Ye for taking the platform to the accuracy frontier. He lists the continuity reading with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the pending redefinition of the second as his own reservations, and he keeps B010 and B061 as possible second parts. He has also disclosed a doctoral research stay in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with your division of roles and I think a citation stating the invention and its development covers it without ranking the two contributions. On your Hall disclosure, I would not call it disqualifying. A stay in a laboratory of a 2005 laureate does not make you a party to the Katori and Ye case, and your own text states the continuity objection against B040 rather than shading it. That candour is why your assessment of distinctness is useful to the rest of us, and I would let you take part, noting the disclosure in the record. On a second part, I do not see one that clears the bar. B010 is protocol-level and has the 2022 overlap Mehlig describes, and B061 still cannot be credited correctly within three names, so for me a single part is the more defensible configuration.

responses.point: Mehlig set aside his own first choice, KPZ (B005), because it has no committee support and the exact-solution contributors are outside the credited names, and now prefers B040 with a citation around the invention and development of the optical lattice clock rather than record figures. He says the lattice-clock concept and its record accuracy are separable and specific.
responses.response: I agree that the concept and the accuracy record are separable, and that is why I would not put a figure such as 1e-18 in the citation. Records get superseded and the citation should outlast them. Where I would go slightly further is on the physical principle: a bare statement of invention and development risks reading as general clock progress, which is the continuity argument you and Kroll flag. Naming the magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms makes the distinction from 2005 and 2012 explicit. I also share your conclusion about B005. I set aside my own B022 for a similar reason, namely that I could not state it in one sentence as a discovery or invention with clean attribution, so I do not see a route for either ballot this year.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved B040 from second to first and asked whether the citation should be species-neutral, name strontium, or divide roles between Katori and Ye, and whether Katori and Ye are an acceptable two-name credit given Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the groups at NIST, PTB and SYRTE. Pearce keeps B018 and B035 as alternatives.
responses.response: On the wording, I prefer the species-neutral form, naming the magic-wavelength optical lattice and the clock, because naming strontium ties the citation to the first realisation and invites a dispute with the ytterbium and other work that followed. A division of roles also works, but it risks ranking two contributions the evidence cannot rank for us. On the credit, I accept two names as the most defensible core: the supplied evidence gives me no ground to add a third, and the record should simply acknowledge the wider community. On your fallback alternatives, I do not agree that B035 would be a safer fallback. Any three of the four Higgs names would leave out someone with a decisive role, which is a structural attribution problem rather than a matter of timing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee ultimately accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-system prizes, and whether the citation wording makes that distinction visible.

How to weigh Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups against the two credited names, and how to divide credit between Katori and Ye, which I cannot settle from the supplied evidence.
Whether Danielsson and others who put discovery of a new channel above enabling invention will accept B040, or whether B018 will keep a separate following.
My judgment on precision-metrology priority depends on the atomic-physics members, since my own field is condensed-matter theory.
statement.conflict_note: Updated: my profile shows a close personal connection to B022 (DMFT and DFT+DMFT lie near my own research on electronic structure), and I no longer prefer it, so no recusal is needed on my preferred configuration; I would still recuse from any decision to prefer B022. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to B040, B061 or B018, or to Katori, Ye, Halzen or Karle.
